Educational Objectives

Robotics & Embedded Systems — Boards Portfolio

Boards is a separate graduation portfolio from my Student Innovation Project (SIP). Each of the six program objectives requires evidence from two distinct projects. A single project may support no more than two objectives. The assignments below are proposed evidence selections, not yet faculty-approved completions.

Boards Objectives and Project Evidence

Each objective is shown word for word, followed by two projects explaining how their work supports it. Projects may be used for at most two objectives. Some matches are provisional; incomplete work is labeled clearly.

Objective 1

Design and complete robotic and embedded systems solutions that apply to real-world situations and challenges.

Project 1: Well Killer SIP

I applied embedded system design to the real-world challenge of shutting down distant irrigation wells during severe weather. I integrated Arduino controllers, a Nextion touchscreen, LoRa communications, and a relay interface. Bench tests verified command transmission, relay activation, and simulated feedback, demonstrating an engineered response to a specific agricultural problem. Connection to a running engine has not yet been validated.

Project 2: Mini Robotic Arm

I designed and 3D-printed a robotic arm, integrated Arduino control, servos and sensors, and progressed from manual motion testing to a completed automatic object-pickup demonstration. The final version uses seven servos and ultrasonic detection, showing mechanical assembly, embedded programming, troubleshooting, and coordinated motion.

Objective 2

Implement a simple microprocessor using digital logic design.

Project 1: Arduino Simon Says Game

I programmed the Arduino Uno ATmega328P to read digital buttons, generate and store sequences, drive LED outputs, and compare input against the stored pattern. This demonstrates processor-controlled digital logic, state sequencing, and awareness of limited embedded memory. The project programs an existing microcontroller rather than constructing a processor from logic gates.

Watch demonstration on YouTube

Circuit diagram and source code

View source code on GitHub

Project 2: 4-Bit Hexadecimal Seven-Segment Display

I implemented binary input interpretation and hexadecimal output decoding: four digital inputs form a 4-bit value, and software selects the corresponding active-low segment pattern. This provides direct evidence of digital logic concepts and microcontroller I/O implementation. Together with Simon Says, it demonstrates introductory processor and digital-logic skills, not a custom-built CPU.

Objective 3

Demonstrate embedded system design skills, including, but not limited to, microcontroller selection, schematic design, printed circuit board layout, design for electromagnetic compatibility and design for manufacturing.

Project 1: Well Killer SIP

I selected Arduino Nano controllers and UART LoRa modules for remote operation, documented the signal and power interfaces, and designed a relay-based connection intended to work alongside the existing Murphy safety controls. This demonstrates microcontroller selection, system-level wiring design, and consideration of installation constraints. A custom PCB, EMC qualification, and production manufacturing review have not been completed.

Project 2: Mini Robotic Arm

I integrated an Arduino Uno, seven servo motors, an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, and separate power supplies. The Arduino receives USB power from a laptop, while the servos use a USB power bank; the grounds are connected. I troubleshot wiring and power distribution to make the hardware and software work together. Objective 4

Apply knowledge of transducers, actuators and simultaneous hardware and software development in the design of an embedded system.

Project 1: Motor Testing and PWM Control Lab

I interfaced the Arduino Uno with an L293D H-bridge to drive two DC motor actuators, and developed firmware to change direction and ramp speed with PWM. I tested electrical control and motor behavior together, demonstrating simultaneous hardware and software development. The control was open-loop rather than sensor-feedback regulated.

Watch demonstration on YouTube

Circuit diagram and source code

View source code on GitHub

Project 2: Potentiometer and Photoresistor Lab

I used the Arduino ADC to convert potentiometer and photoresistor signals into values that control LED outputs, with a switch selecting the active sensor. This demonstrates transducer input acquisition, calibration and mapping of sensor readings, and coordinated circuit and program development. Combined with the motor lab, the two projects cover sensing and actuation.

Objective 5

Design and analyze real-time embedded systems, including advanced digital logic design, signal processing and highspeed digital systems.

Project 1: Arduino Simon Says Game

I implemented a timed, event-driven interaction using button sampling, LED sequences, and program state transitions. This demonstrates the relationship between embedded timing, digital I/O, and responsive behavior. The project does not establish hard real-time deadlines or high-speed digital performance.

Project 2: 4-Bit Hexadecimal Seven-Segment Display

I designed a continuously updated 4-bit input decoder that responds to switch states by driving seven digital outputs. This illustrates deterministic digital logic and repeated input processing. Timing analysis, signal processing, and high-speed digital design would require additional evidence, so this pairing remains provisional.

Objective 6

Implement and evaluate algorithms and methods enabling autonomy in a mobile robot

Project 1: Automatic Object Pickup Robotic Arm — Completed

I completed an automatic object-pickup routine using a stationary Arduino Uno robotic arm with seven servos controlling six joints and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor. When the sensor detects an object 5–20 cm away in three consecutive readings, the arm performs a calibrated sequence to open its gripper, lower, grasp, lift, lower, release, and return upright. This demonstrates sensor-triggered autonomous operation and coordinated actuator control. The arm uses fixed programmed poses, not ultrasonic mapping or independent path planning, and it is not a mobile robot.

Evidence and Next Steps

Completed coursework provides a foundation for Boards, but the objective-specific evidence and faculty review remain in progress.

Completed coursework

Robotic arm, seven-segment display, motor control, potentiometer/photoresistor, sensor, and Simon game labs. Collect original code, schematics, lab reports, and screenshots.

Well Killer SIP

Bench-tested LoRa messaging, Nextion control, relay pulse, and simulated optocoupler feedback. Actual Murphy/engine shutdown has not been validated. Use this project for Objectives 1 and 4 only.

Objective 4

Add explicit evaluation of use cases, design alternatives, limitations, and tradeoffs for the SIP and sensor lab.

Objective 5 — evidence gap

The Simon and motor-control labs are candidates, not confirmed demonstrations of autonomy. Identify or implement autonomous mechanical behavior before claiming this objective is met.

Objective 6 — planned

Assignments 4.1 (voice) and 4.2 (vision) are due November 23. Integrate AI output with a robotic platform or simulation and document tests. They are not complete yet.

Revision deadline

Target initial evidence assembly by November 23 and complete revisions by approximately November 26, 2026.
